strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive and systematic study of attentive probing methods under a unified mathematical framework. This clarifies and benchmarks a scattered set of methods (from probing to pooling) in a fair and rigorous manner.

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) is conceptually simple, elegant, and highly effective. By optimizing learnable queries directly in the input feature space, it completely eliminates key and query projections, achieving up to 10x compute speedup (GFLOPs) and massive parameter reduction.

Extensive and thorough experiments across seven diverse datasets (ImageNet-1k, CIFAR-100, Places365, etc.), multiple pretraining paradigms (MIM, JEA, VLMs), and different backbone scales (ViT-S/B/L) demonstrate the generality and robustness of the proposed method.
The analysis linking attention localization quality (and entropy) to classification accuracy provides solid scientific insights into why the method works.

Strong performance is demonstrated in low-shot regimes (closing ~71-75% of the LP-to-FT gap) and layer-wise probing (maintaining much higher accuracy in intermediate layers compared to standard linear probing).
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat limited/incremental, as the main architectural change is the simplification of standard cross-attention by removing projection layers and utilizing direct learnable queries.

While the paper positions attentive probing as an alternative to fine-tuning, it lacks direct empirical comparison with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA or Adapters. Since PEFT is also widely used to avoid full fine-tuning with low parameter/compute overhead, comparing EP against PEFT (under similar trainable parameter constraints) would make the evaluation more comprehensive.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and timely topic: the evaluation of self-supervised vision representations, particularly for masked image modeling (MIM) where standard linear probing often falls short.

The unified mathematical formulation in Section 3 is excellent. It neatly structures and categorizes various seemingly distinct attention-based pooling methods (such as AIM, SimPool, V-JEPA, AbMILP, etc.) into a cohesive framework.

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) method is elegant and simple. By removing unnecessary key transformations and directly learning queries in the input representation space, it significantly reduces parameters and computational complexity (up to 10x speedup) while matching or exceeding the performance of heavier alternatives.

The experimental evaluation is highly comprehensive, spanning seven datasets, four different MIM models, multiple backbone scales (ViT-S, B, L), and diverse pre-training paradigms (including JEA, Hybrid, and VL models).

The paper provides insightful analysis, such as the correlation between classification accuracy and attention localization/entropy, and includes extensive and high-quality qualitative visualizations of the query-specific attention maps.
weaknesses: From a purely algorithmic perspective, the novelty of EP is somewhat incremental, as it primarily consists of simplifying cross-attention by removing projection layers and utilizing learnable queries (highly reminiscent of a single-iteration Slot Attention without routing).

While the paper frames attentive probing as a lightweight alternative to full fine-tuning and discusses PEFT in the related work, it lacks empirical comparisons to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA. Comparing the accuracy-efficiency trade-offs of EP against a low-rank adapter on the ViT backbone would provide useful context for practitioners deciding between probing and PEFT.
There is a minor typo on page 13, Section C.2: 'As shown in Figure 9a and Figure 9a...' which should likely refer to Figure 9a and 9b.

strengths: Unified Formulation and Systematic Survey: The paper provides a very clean, unified mathematical framework (Section 3) that harmonizes a wide range of attentive pooling and probing methods (such as AIM, CAE, V-JEPA, SimPool, AbMILP, DELF, and CBAM). This significantly clarifies the relationships between these seemingly disparate approaches.

Strong Empirical Efficiency & Accuracy: The proposed 'Efficient Probing' (EP) eliminates redundant key/query projection matrices, resulting in up to a 10× speedup in GFLOPs over conventional multi-head attention probing, while maintaining or exceeding state-of-the-art accuracy.

Extensive and Diverse Benchmarking: The evaluation spans 7 diverse classification datasets (including ImageNet-1k, CIFAR-100, Places365, and several fine-grained tasks) and covers multiple self-supervised pre-training paradigms (MIM, Joint-Embedding, Hybrid, and Vision-Language). The paper also conducts robust layer-wise and low-shot analyses.

Insightful Interpretability Analysis: The manuscript presents a compelling quantitative analysis connecting downstream classification performance to the localization quality (overlap with ground-truth bounding boxes) and entropy of the attention maps. The qualitative visualizations demonstrate that the learned queries successfully decompose objects into semantically meaningful, complementary parts without explicit supervision.
weaknesses: Limited Algorithmic Novelty: From a purely technical standpoint, the proposed EP method is a highly simplified version of cross-attention (i.e., removing query and key projection matrices and setting queries to direct learnable vectors). While this simplicity is a practical advantage, the conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental.

Lack of Empirical Comparison with PEFT: Although the authors discuss the conceptual connection to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) in Appendix A, a direct empirical comparison with lightweight PEFT techniques (such as LoRA or Adapters applied to the backbone) is missing. Comparing EP with these methods on the same downstream tasks would provide a more comprehensive view of the accuracy-efficiency trade-off when adapting frozen backbones.

Training Overhead and Convergence: While EP is extremely efficient in terms of parameters and GFLOPs, the evaluation protocol still requires training the probing layers for 90 epochs. A discussion or comparison regarding the wall-clock training convergence time relative to standard linear probing (which often converges in fewer epochs) would be beneficial.

strengths: Presents a highly valuable, unified framework that conceptualizes and mathematically aligns diverse attentive probing methods (such as MHCA, AbMILP, AIM, DELF, SimPool, V-JEPA) under a single notation, which greatly clarifies the design space.

Proposes a simple, intuitive, and highly efficient probing mechanism (EP) by eliminating redundant query and key projections. This reduces parameter counts and GFLOPs significantly while matching or outperforming heavier alternatives.
Provides an exceptionally thorough evaluation across 15 different pre-training models (including MIM, Joint-Embedding, VLMs, and generative architectures) and 7 diverse classification datasets.

Includes deep and insightful analyses, such as demonstrating a clear correlation between spatial localization/entropy and predictive performance, and introducing a quantitative 'complementarity score' to evaluate query specialization.
The paper is very well-written, clear, and includes beautiful and informative visualizations of attention maps and Pareto frontiers.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (using learnable query vectors directly in the representation space without key/query transformations) has low conceptual novelty, as it is very closely related to static slot attention, query-based pooling, or Perceiver-style architectures.

While the paper analyzes GFLOPs for the probing head, the backbone forward pass (e.g., 17.58 GFLOPs for ViT-B) heavily dominates the overall computation. Thus, the relative end-to-end wall-clock time savings during training/inference might be minor compared to existing attentive probes.

As probing methods become more expressive and introduce more trainable parameters (e.g., EP64 has ~1.4M parameters), the boundary between pure probing (evaluating existing representations) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) becomes slightly blurred.

strengths: The paper provides a strong unifying framework that systematizes several existing but disparate attentive pooling/probing methods (e.g., AIM, SimPool, V-JEPA) under a single mathematical formulation (Table 1).

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) is elegantly simple. By removing the query/key projections and directly learning queries in the feature space, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across 7 benchmarks and diverse pre-training paradigms (MIM, JEA, VLM, Generative).

The experimental evaluation is highly thorough and robust, comparing against many baselines and covering multiple pre-training architectures (including MAE, BEiTv2, DINOv2, CLIP, SigLIP, and DiT) across various parameter budgets and FLOPs.

The paper includes very insightful diagnostic analyses, demonstrating a strong correlation between attention localization (entropy) and accuracy, and showing that EP learns highly complementary attention maps corresponding to distinct semantic parts of objects.
The exploration of Matryoshka representation learning to achieve multi-scale probing without training separate classifiers is a clever and practical contribution.
weaknesses: The core idea of using learned query vectors to perform cross-attention pooling on frozen features is conceptually close to existing attention poolers, Slot Attention, or query-based architectures (e.g., DETR, Perceiver), which slightly limits the overall architectural novelty.

A practical challenge of patch-level attentive probing (including EP) compared to standard linear probing (LP) is the storage and memory footprint. In standard LP, one can pre-compute and store a single global token vector (e.g., [CLS]) for the entire dataset to enable extremely fast classifier training. In contrast, attentive probing requires either storing all patch tokens (which is $196\times$ larger for a typical $14\times14$ ViT) or running the backbone forward pass on-the-fly. The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of this representation-storage trade-off.

strengths: The paper provides the first comprehensive and systematic study of attentive probing, unifying diverse existing methods (such as AIM, V-JEPA, CAE, and SimPool) under a single, cohesive framework (neatly summarized in Section 3 and Table 1).

The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) is simple yet highly parameter- and compute-efficient. For a probing protocol—where minimizing the overhead on top of a frozen backbone is paramount—this simplicity and efficiency are highly desirable.

The paper features exceptionally thorough experimental validation, evaluating 15 pre-training models across five distinct paradigms (MIM, JEA, hybrid, VLMs, generative) and testing them across 7 different image classification benchmarks.

It offers highly insightful analysis regarding the attention maps, demonstrating a clear correlation between spatial localization/entropy and classification accuracy, and uncovering the emergence of diverse, complementary attention maps.

The paper is exceptionally well-written, organized, and polished, with outstanding visualizations and an extensive appendix that details additional configurations and analyses (like layer-wise and low-shot probing).
weaknesses: The technical and algorithmic novelty is relatively straightforward, as EP essentially simplifies standard cross-attention by removing key and query projection matrices and learning queries directly in the input feature space.

The performance and parameter/FLOP trade-offs depend on the hyperparameter configurations of the number of queries (M) and output dimension (Do), which requires some manual selection based on the target resource budget.

The evaluation is restricted to frozen backbones on standard image classification. The synergy of EP with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and its applicability to dense downstream tasks (like object detection or segmentation) are left mostly as future work.

strengths: Comprehensive and Unified Framework: The paper successfully unifies diverse attention-based pooling and probing methods under a single mathematical framework (Table 1), making it easy to compare and contrast prior work.

Simple and Elegant Solution: The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) method is simple yet mathematically sound. By absorbing key projection matrices into learnable query vectors directly in the input space, it dramatically reduces parameter counts and compute overhead without sacrificing performance.

Extensive and Rigorous Evaluation: The experimental setup is extremely thorough, evaluating 15 different pre-trained models (across MIM, JEA, VLMs, and generative paradigms) on multiple benchmarks. The inclusion of downstream tasks like unsupervised object localization and zero-shot retrieval showcases the versatility of EP.

Insightful Empirical Discoveries: The paper uncovers valuable properties, such as the correlation between spatial localization and classification performance, the high semantic complementarity of EP's attention maps, and its synergy when paired with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT/LoRA).

Excellent Clarity and Visualization: The paper is exceptionally well-written, featuring highly illustrative figures and tables that make the concepts, methods, and comparative results very easy to digest.
weaknesses: Incremental Core Methodology: While the empirical analysis, benchmarking, and unification are highly comprehensive, the core architectural modification (simplifying cross-attention by learning queries directly in the feature space and eliminating projections) is somewhat incremental.

Lack of Theoretical Explanation for High Complementarity: Although the paper successfully demonstrates and quantifies that EP's queries yield more complementary and diverse attention maps, it lacks a deeper theoretical explanation or intuition as to why removing key projection matrices causes this self-diversification compared to standard MHCA.

Training Wall-Clock Time: While EP is parameter-efficient and computationally lightweight during inference, training attention maps over 90 epochs is still significantly more expensive than standard linear probing on cached features. Highlighting the exact training wall-clock time differences would help contextualize the practical trade-off.

strengths: Clean and unified mathematical framework: The paper successfully unifies multiple existing attentive pooling/probing methods (e.g., AIM, V-JEPA, SimPool, DELF) into a single, cohesive framework, clearly highlighting where parameter and computational redundancies lie.

Simple, elegant, and mathematically sound method: The proposed Efficient Probing (EP) elegantly replaces the key projection matrix and query vectors with a single learnable query vector per head (using the equivalence $u_j = W_{Kj}^\top q_j$). This mathematical equivalence allows a massive reduction in parameter counts and FLOPs without any loss in representational capacity.

Extensive and rigorous benchmarking: The evaluation is exceptionally thorough, spanning 15 pre-trained models (encompassing MIM, JEA, VLM, and Generative paradigms) across 8 diverse datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, Places365, and several fine-grained classification tasks). EP consistently defines the Pareto frontier of accuracy-vs-parameters and accuracy-vs-compute.

Insightful analytical results: The analysis of emerging properties—specifically, the spatial localization of attention queries, lower attention entropy, and higher complementarity (diversity) of attention maps—adds strong scientific and interpretability value to the paper.

Integration with PEFT: The demonstration that EP is synergistic with LoRA (yielding a hybrid LoRA + EP configuration that dominates both pure probing and pure LoRA) is a highly practical and interesting finding.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty: Although the mathematical simplification of the attention query is elegant and highly effective, the core mechanism is still a variant of standard cross-attention pooling (similar to slot attention or query-based pooling). The concept of using learnable queries to pool patch tokens is already quite established in the literature.

Philosophical boundary of probing: Utilizing a ~1M parameter attentive probe slightly blurs the classical definition of 'probing' as a simple diagnostic protocol designed to measure the intrinsic quality of frozen representations. More expressive probes run the risk of 'repairing' or adjusting representations rather than purely evaluating them, though the authors partially address this by evaluating EP at ultra-low parameter budgets (e.g., ~200k parameters).

Practical wall-clock training efficiency: In real-world workflows, standard linear probing is popular because backbone features can be pre-computed and cached once to avoid expensive forward passes. When combining EP with PEFT (like LoRA) or when evaluating across multiple layers, this caching advantage is lost. A more detailed discussion on wall-clock training time and caching trade-offs in the main text would have been helpful.

strengths: Highly comprehensive and systematic evaluation across 15 pre-trained models from 5 distinct paradigms (MIM, JEA, VLMs, AR, and diffusion) and multiple datasets, establishing a much-needed unified benchmark for attentive probing.

Elegant and well-justified mathematical simplification that collapses query and key projections into direct learnable query vectors $u_j$. This drastically reduces parameters and FLOPs while preserving the mathematical expressivity of the attention mechanism.
Exceptional accuracy-efficiency trade-off, consistently dominating the Pareto frontier over previous probing and pooling methods.
Demonstrated multi-task utility: the learned attention maps generalize 'out-of-the-box' to unsupervised object localization and zero-shot image retrieval without further training.

Thorough and insightful analytical experiments exploring emerging properties, including attention entropy, query complementarity, Matryoshka representation learning, and layer-wise probing robustness.
weaknesses: The core methodological innovation is somewhat incremental, as simplifying cross-attention by learning query vectors directly in the feature space is a known concept in slot attention and prototype-based models.

The distinction between a 'probe' and a lightweight parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method is slightly blurred. Since EP trains multiple value projection matrices $W_{Vj}$ alongside the queries, it acts more like a lightweight task-specific head rather than a pure, passive probe of the pre-existing representations.

As noted in the limitations, training the probe still incurs a heavy backbone forward-pass cost during optimization unless features are pre-cached, which limits the real-world speedup of the training phase itself.
